title: The Body of Death and the Nature of the Soul
english: He finds pleasure in the burden of wickedness rather, and distances himself from Jesus. For this reason it is also said in Isaiah: 'Egypt has grown weary, the commerce of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans, lofty men, shall pass over you and shall be your servants and shall worship you, for God strengthens and there is no god besides you' (Isa 18:7). 'Egypt has grown weary' at the time when those who are of the wicked have received sensation, practicing idolatry and possessing idle chatter regarding curious things, regarding augury, regarding necromancy, and the demons lying near them. But when they do not have sensation of these, they do not grow weary. 'The commerce' therefore 'of the Ethiopians' or 'the trades of the Ethiopians' grows weary then. And 'Ethiopians' refers to those darkened according to the inner man.

Thus also the devil in the Epistle of Barnabas and in the Shepherd is called 'the black one,' not according to the body, but having been darkened according to the mind, having become outside the brightness of the saints. These therefore the Ethiopians have a journey or a way, where their commerce is. And they grow weary then when they receive sensation, for howsoever one finds pleasure in sinning, he does not grow weary.

'They swelled and my sores decayed from the face of my folly' (Ps 38:3). I had sores from the arrows of punishment or from the burning arrows of the evil one; for it has also been said to have burning arrows. When someone receives impressions, that is, thoughts and memories of evils and impieties, he is in a sore. But when these have increased and having become unburdened they swell, then they also undergo putrefaction. 'They swelled' therefore 'and my sores decayed.' But from where did I have the sores, from where has their putrefaction happened? — 'from the face of my folly.' It is necessary to expose my folly and to turn away from it. Someone undergoes folly when he does not possess prudence.

The stings of thoughts and of desires, these make sores. It is necessary to heal these quickly. Someone saw a woman toward desire; he had a sore. Let him heal, and until the passion, let him set the anger in order; for in this way neither desire shall swell nor bring putrefaction. But when the mind remains, these bring both putrefaction and stench and uncleanness. When he does not have this prudence so as to know what ought to be done and what not, having the things said in a mixed way as indifferent, in...

It is in folly. And folly, regarding those things that boast of being small sins so as to compare them to madness, nourishes and strengthens, and becomes a stench and corruption. Likewise, regarding the essence of which the word is spoken, it takes the resemblance and the corruption; for nothing bodily appears; for many foolish people are healthy and have strong bodies.

I was wretched and was bowed down to the end. The unseemly and burdensome things often bring wretchedness. And the body itself indeed makes the one burdened wretched. This concept is submitted by the apostolic word which has it thus: 'Wretched am I, man; who will rescue me from the body of this death?' (Romans 7:24). Since indeed I am in the body of death, I am wretched, and not by chance will the Savior make me out of such wretchedness; for he immediately brought forward: 'I give thanks through Jesus Christ' (Romans 7:25), who freed me from the body. We say, therefore, that wretchedness comes to the soul from the body of death.

We do not at once take the body of death to be any body, but a body of this kind. When someone uses this body as if to do sins toward death, a body of death remains surrounding him. But it is possible to make it not a body of death; for when I separate from it those things making it a body of death, it is no longer a body of death. And just as this perceptible body has underlying matter and the form of a body, it is possible to separate this body from the thick body. When it takes only the three dimensions without matter, this body is not essence.

In these readily available things, when it is said, for example, 'color in body,' does it not also mean 'in a certain body,' because by saying 'color in body' it showed that this body means the seen thing, which we touch? But when it says a single form is the quantity of the body, it does not say this; for how can an essence be a genus of essence? So the body is homonymous: for that which is taken according to the three dimensions without matter, this is the quantitative body; for that with matter, we take not only the dimensions but also the underlying essence with them. This body is something else. The body, therefore, is then a body of death, when those things working in it and its movements happen sinfully. It is possible, therefore, to separate this from...

title: The Lessons of Sin and the Desires of the Soul
english: Regarding the body: when I take an eye that does not see, seeing in a harmful or adulterous way, I have removed the eye of death from the essence. And upon every member and upon every sense, if this happens, the body of death is cast off. It is not the body we cast off, but the body of death. And if we see a worthless man having changed into a significant one, we say that the worthless man was destroyed, not the man.

'And we were bowed down.' Lowly wickedness is, it bows down the one possessing it; for always the great sorrows lie upon one, crushing and bowing down the one carrying them. Immediately, indeed, regarding her who had that 'spirit of infirmity' for eighteen years, it says: 'she was bent over and could not raise herself to the full.' She never raised herself up. The one sinning, therefore, bends down and looks below. It says, therefore: 'they set their eyes to bend down toward the earth' (Ps 118:25); and again in Jeremiah it is said: 'having turned away upon the earth they have written' (Jer 17:13). Those having turned away from the divine spring are written of, being enrolled in the earth, as having the citizenship below and bearing 'the image of the jar' (cf. 2 Tim 2:20). But of the disciples, 'the names are written in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). He does not speak of these designations by combining letters, but of the very qualities which signify them, for the definition of a name is given thus: a name is a principal designation representing the quality of the one named. This is the descriptive name: man, heaven. 'Is written,' therefore, that is, has been arranged.

7 I was walking, mourning all the day. Even if 'I was bowed down to the end' because of the approaching misery, I did not become insensitive to this. Mourning, therefore, I walk, 'working the godliness according to God, the sorrow leading to repentance unto salvation without regret' (2 Cor 7:10). And so mourning I walk all the day. And the 'I walk' is good. It does not remain cast down, but it walks. It did not 'sink down to earth in sitting,' it did not set its transferred habits upon the earth, but it walks. 'Mourning,' therefore, 'I was walking.' Those things were working which were transferring me out of the misery. Then, however, I am transferred out of the misery, if I cast off the causes of the misery. 8 For my soul was filled with instructions. My soul was filled with sins. And instructions are...

Regarding sins: the deceiver plays with the deceived, and thus the soul is filled with lessons. In some copies, it says 'my loins.' It is said concerning these that the seeds consist. When someone is thus drawn into lawlessness and hastens more toward lust or toward being a lover of God, he has the loins filled with lessons.

“And there is no healing in my flesh” (Ps 32:18). As long as I am filled with these lessons, not only is my flesh not healthy, but having become diseased and thus disposed, it does not receive healing. Just as it is impossible for a sensory person, while still in the state of being sick, to recover health, so the one filled with lessons is not able to make the flesh peaceful, that is, sober, or not divided against itself.

“I was afflicted and humbled exceedingly” (Ps 32:3). It is possible to say 'I was afflicted and humbled' voluntarily. Since I have become in sensation of the swelling of evil and harm and blindness, I led myself volitionally toward humiliation so that I might be exalted; for “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Mt 23:12). One must take the affliction and the humiliation from a parallel source. But then it happens voluntarily when, as I have said, the one who was exalted humbles himself, so that he might be exalted by God. It is also possible in this way: from the surrounding oppressors and heavy burdens, “I was humbled, I was afflicted exceedingly.” I had the affliction stretched out.

“I cried out from the sighing of my heart” (Ps 34:1). Not mockingly wailing about the evils surrounding me, but “from the sighing of my heart”; understanding in what kind of sighing one must sigh, a sigh.

“And all my desire is against you” (Ps 38:9). The righteous man always has love and longing for the virtues and for things done praiseworthily. It is indeed said concerning the righteous: “All the desire of the righteous is good” (Ps 37:4). And the good things have the boldness to be additional to God. “Against you,” therefore, that is, before you, is “all my desire.” Praise is therefore to be taken here for “my desire,” which is also what this same one says: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things” (Ps 103:5). All such desires, being the righteous, are bold to be additional to God. But it is also possible to take the word toward the other meaning. Because...

title: The Light of Knowledge and the Strength of the Heart
english: This person was humbled and was utterly crushed; because of this, I am consumed, and my groaning comes from soul and heart, since I have come to know that every bad desire I possessed is manifest to you, and no desire is outside of your presence. The term 'moreover' is more appropriate. 10 And my groaning was not hidden from you. Having a good desire and longing to be in goodness and virtue, I groan as much as I see myself failing. This groaning, however, comes from a desire for beauty, from the expectation of something better. Even if I often hide my groaning from many, so that I might not seem to be self-indulgent and appear to be repenting only outwardly, my groaning is 'moreover' to you; it was not hidden from you. The Egyptians indeed oppressed the Hebrews. When the 'sons of Israel' (Exodus 2:23) rejoiced in the works of the Egyptians, their groaning was hidden from the face of God. But when they began to groan over the works, when they perceived that the Pharaonic works were destroying both the land and, even more, were doing [evil] outside of God, then they groaned, and the groaning was not hidden from God; for He immediately set them free. When they were rejoicing, they were held there, and they did not attain freedom. This groaning corresponds to 'the sorrow that works repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10). This sorrow is another from that of the world, which works death. If, indeed, you see a man groaning because he does not attain what he desires, even if they are bad things, this groaning is destructive.

11 My heart was troubled, and my strength left me. When the heart is troubled, that is, the mind, then strength becomes distant. Strength is that which is appropriate to the peace and stability of the heart. He who learned from Jesus 'that He is gentle and humble in heart' (Matthew 11:29) does not have a troubled heart; for he imitates Jesus. And he who imitates Jesus is outside of all trouble. Until he does not have this trouble, strength remains with him, so as to say: 'I can do all things in Him who strengthens me' (Philippians 4:13), and: 'I will love you, Lord, my strength' (Psalm 18:1). 11 And the light of my eyes is not with me. The light of my eyes has become distant from me. But the light of the true eyes...

For those seeing sharply, the knowledge of truth is present; for it has been said: 'light up for yourselves a light of knowledge' (Ps 119:130). For the word is not about these eyes nor about sensible light; listen to the one saying: 'the commandment of the Lord is far-reaching, enlightening eyes' (Ps 119:105). Indeed, the keeping of the far-reaching commandment enlightens the eyes of the inner man; for many are those seeing sharply, yet they are transgressors of the commandment of the Lord, and they guard it in a different way, and being encompassed by it, they are dull according to the appearance.

It is not, therefore, at all about the eyes that it is said: 'and the light of my eyes is not with me' (Ps 38:11). He has left me, because I turned away from it, because I myself did not guard it to remain with me. 'My heart was troubled, my strength left me' (Ps 38:10). When the intellect is troubled, if it endures, strength becomes far-reaching; for when the intellect is strengthened and the mind is made precise, strength is present to one thus disposed, as to say: 'I am strong in all things in the one empowering me' (Phil 4:13). 'I will love you, Lord, my strength.' But one is left behind by this strength if, when troubled, he endures in the heart, if he has troubling thoughts. Therefore, it must be guarded not to give 'a place to the devil' to the one casting disturbances, so that our strength may remain and we may be able to say: 'The Lord is my strength and my song, and he became for me salvation' (Ps 28:7).

'And the light of my eyes is not with me' (Ps 38:11). When the heart is troubled, the strength appropriate to the heart leaves it, and that very light is not with the one having suffered these things; for it is necessary to 'sow into righteousness and reap into a fruit of life' (Gal 6:7), so that, 'having lightened for themselves a light of knowledge' (Ps 119:130). Therefore, when the heart is troubled, the strength that empowers the inner man becomes distant, and that very light of the eyes which enlightens the inner man leaves him, having delivered himself to darkness and ignorance.

'My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood opposite me' (Ps 41:9). Such things happen in circumstantial times. And Job, having been born in distress, said such things: 'My friends have become merciless, they have known [others] as three times more than I' (Job 19:14). And in the Wisdoms it has been written that friends only then [fail] and the [goodness] of friends...
